prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, taking atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 regime

statement.case_for: After reading all eight openings I still place optical lattice clocks first. Four of eight members put B022 first and it is the only candidate that combines a single sharply defined invention (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, Katori) with its realisation at record accuracy and stability (Ye), a clean two-person credit, and a decade or more of independent confirmation by several laboratories comparing clocks over fibre links. It is a discovery in the sense that matters for an instrument-level prize: it changes what can be measured and how accurately, and it is already being used for tests of fundamental constants, searches for new physics, relativistic geodesy and the discussion of redefining the second. Its maturity is not in doubt, and the credited pair is more compact than any of the topological, quantum-information or cosmology alternatives.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier metrology prizes: frequency combs (Hall and Hansch, 2005) and single-ion control and the Al+ ion clock (Wineland, 2012). A committee could judge that precision timekeeping has been honoured twice already, and that the lattice clock is an evolution of that lineage. There is also a real attribution question about other lattice-clock contributors (Lemonde, Takamoto and the ytterbium and PTB groups), and the practical culmination, a redefined second, has not yet happened. If the committee prefers a field with more recent, rapidly growing impact, B030 or the topological candidates are the natural competitors.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B022 first but flags that overlap with earlier Nobel-recognised metrology (frequency combs, Wineland ion control) may be argued by some members, and that the SI second has not yet been redefined.
responses.response: I take the overlap seriously, and I think it is answerable. The comb prize recognised the tool that makes optical frequencies countable and the 2012 prize the control of single quantum systems; neither covers the idea that a million neutral atoms can be trapped without a light shift and interrogated simultaneously, which is what gives the statistical gain behind the 10^-18 stability. The citation should therefore be worded narrowly around lattice clocks rather than around optical clocks in general. I also agree that the redefinition of the second is not a prerequisite: the science has already been delivered and does not depend on a metrology-body decision.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks topological insulators (B045, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a new organising principle of electronic phases with a decisive theory-plus-experiment pair, and sees the trio as compact and defensible.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual importance, but I do not find the credit story as compact as stated. Eriksson himself notes that the HgTe proposal is incompletely credited and one proposer is deceased, and Johansson, Lindroth and Mehlig each propose a different trio, with Xue or Hasan swapped in; that spread is itself evidence that the allocation is unsettled. The field also sits close to the 2016 prize on topological phases. I would not oppose a topological prize in principle, and I rank B004 as a serious alternative, but I would want the committee to settle which discovery is being rewarded (quantum spin Hall, 3D insulators, or quantum anomalous Hall) before preferring it over a clean pair.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B030) first as a rare theory-followed-by-experiment discovery that created a large new field, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero as a natural split.
responses.response: I agree that B030 is the cleanest theory-plus-experiment story outside my first choice, and I list it as an alternative. My reservation is maturity: the pairing mechanism is still debated, results are sensitive to twist-angle disorder, and, as Danielsson's own uncertainty notes, other twistronics and experimental groups complicate the attribution. A Nobel Prize for a discovery that has stood for only seven or eight years in a still-moving field is possible, but I would rather reward a case where the interpretation has stopped shifting. I would not object strongly if the committee concluded the field is ready.

responses.point: Johansson ranks quantum spin Hall (B004, Kane and Molenkamp) first and circuit QED (B039) second, while noting that proximity to the 2025 superconducting-circuits prize may argue for waiting and disclosing a Chalmers link to the cQED community.
responses.response: I agree with the argument for waiting on B039 given the 2025 prize, and I appreciate that the Chalmers connection is disclosed as a bias rather than used as evidence. On B004 I note that Johansson, unlike the other B004 proposers, would limit the credit to Kane and Molenkamp, which is a cleaner configuration than the one with Xue. That does not change my preference, but it would make B004 a stronger fallback than its three-name form suggests.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee will give to overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes when judging a further precision-metrology award.

Whether other lattice-clock contributors (for example Lemonde, Takamoto, the ytterbium and PTB groups) are sufficiently decisive to challenge a Katori-Ye pair; this rests on my recollection of the priority history.
Whether the committee would rather wait for the redefinition of the second, which I do not consider necessary but others might.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall is a 2005 laureate in the same precision-spectroscopy area as the lattice clocks; Jun Ye is a Hall-lineage JILA scientist, so a personal or institutional connection to the B022 field may require the committee to consider recusal. I am not aware of a direct collaboration with Katori or Ye in my profile, and I have no documented connection to the other shortlisted candidates, although my Lund atomic-physics and quantum-information work lies close to B008 and B033.
